conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.front: What is the progestogen-only pill (POP), and when is it the go-to oral method?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.back: A daily oral contraceptive containing only a progestogen (no oestrogen). It is the go-to oral method when oestrogen is contraindicated — i.e. the situations that make the COCP UKMEC 3/4: VTE history, migraine with aura, age >35 and smoking, hypertension, breastfeeding.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.front: What is the core trade-off of the POP compared with the COCP?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.back: No oestrogen → no oestrogen-related risks (VTE, arterial disease) → far broader eligibility. But the cost is less forgiving daily timing and less predictable bleeding.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.front: What is the mechanism of action of traditional POPs (levonorgestrel, norethisterone)?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.back: Mainly thickening cervical mucus (a barrier to sperm), plus endometrial thinning and reduced tubal motility. They inhibit ovulation in only ~50–60% of cycles, so the mucus effect is the mainstay — and it is short-lived, hence the strict 3-hour window.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.front: How do desogestrel and drospirenone POPs differ mechanistically from traditional POPs?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.back: They also reliably inhibit ovulation (in addition to the mucus effect). This makes them more effective and allows a longer missed-pill window (e.g. the desogestrel POP's anovulatory action is why it has a 12-hour window).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.front: What is the missed-pill window for a TRADITIONAL POP (levonorgestrel, norethisterone)?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.back: It is 'missed' if taken more than 3 hours late.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.front: What is the missed-pill window for the DESOGESTREL POP (Cerazette)?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.back: It is 'missed' if taken more than 12 hours late.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.front: What is the missed-pill window for the DROSPIRENONE POP (Slynd)?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.back: It is 'missed' if taken more than 24 hours late (it also has a 4-day hormone-free interval, with its own rules).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.front: What should a woman do if she misses a POP?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.back: Take the missed pill as soon as possible (even if that means 2 in one day); if more than one is missed, just take the most recent one and continue the pack. Take the next at the usual time, use condoms until pills have been taken correctly for 48 hours, and consider emergency contraception if UPSI occurred during the unprotected window.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.front: Why is the extra-cover period 48 hours after a missed POP or a late start?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.back: Because it takes ~48 hours for cervical mucus to re-thicken to an effective barrier.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.front: What counts as a missed pill in terms of vomiting/diarrhoea with the POP?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.back: Vomiting within 2 hours of taking it, or severe diarrhoea, should be treated as a missed pill.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.front: What are the starting rules for the POP?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.back: Started up to and including day 5 of the cycle → immediate protection. Started at any other time → 48 hours (2 days) of additional contraception.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.front: How can a woman switch from the COCP to the POP with immediate protection?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.back: By continuing directly from the end of an active COCP packet (straight after day 21, with no pill-free gap) → immediate protection.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.front: Is there a pill-free break with the POP?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.back: No — the POP is taken at the same time every day, continuously, with NO pill-free break (unlike the COCP).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.front: Do ordinary (non-enzyme-inducing) antibiotics reduce POP efficacy?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.back: No — this is a common misconception. Ordinary antibiotics do NOT reduce POP efficacy and need no extra precautions.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.front: Which drugs DO reduce POP efficacy, and what should be done?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.back: Enzyme-inducing drugs — rifampicin/rifabutin and other P450 inducers (some anticonvulsants, St John's Wort) — reduce efficacy. Use additional or alternative contraception; a non-hormonal method (e.g. copper IUD) is preferred.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.front: What is the most common side effect of the POP, and the leading reason for discontinuation?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.back: Irregular vaginal bleeding — unpredictable spotting/bleeding or amenorrhoea. If persistent beyond 3 months, exclude other causes (STI, pregnancy, cervical pathology).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.front: List other adverse effects associated with the POP.
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.back: Breast tenderness, weight gain (perceived), acne, headache, mood changes, and a small increased risk of ovarian cysts.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.front: What is the ectopic pregnancy consideration with the traditional POP?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.back: Because the traditional POP does not always stop ovulation, a slightly higher PROPORTION of pregnancies are ectopic → exclude ectopic if a POP user becomes pregnant with pain. (Overall, any contraception lowers the absolute ectopic risk versus none.)

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.front: What is the main UKMEC 4 (absolute) contraindication to the POP?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.back: Current breast cancer.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.front: What are the UKMEC 3 (relative) contraindications to the POP?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.back: Past breast cancer; active/severe liver disease, cirrhosis or liver tumours; stroke or ischaemic heart disease developing while on the method; and unexplained vaginal bleeding before evaluation.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.front: Why is the POP said to have 'few contraindications' as its key advantage?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.back: Because it lacks oestrogen it is usable in almost everyone — including where the COCP is contraindicated (VTE history, migraine with aura, >35 and smoking, hypertension, breastfeeding). Current breast cancer is the main absolute contraindication.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.front: Can the POP be used while breastfeeding?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.back: Yes — it is safe in breastfeeding (UKMEC 1), can be started immediately postpartum, and only a small amount enters milk, which is harmless to the infant.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.front: Why does the traditional POP have a much stricter timing window than the desogestrel/drospirenone POPs?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.back: Because the traditional POP relies mainly on the short-lived cervical-mucus effect (ovulation is inhibited in only ~50–60% of cycles), whereas desogestrel/drospirenone reliably inhibit ovulation, giving a wider safety margin and longer window.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.front: A woman on a traditional POP takes it 2 hours late. Is this a missed pill?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.back: No — for a traditional POP the window is 3 hours, so 2 hours late is fine and no extra precautions are needed. (It would be a missed pill only if >3 hours late.)

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.front: What is intrauterine contraception, and what are the two types?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.back: A small T-shaped device placed inside the uterus for long-acting reversible contraception (LARC). Two types with fundamentally different mechanisms: the copper IUD (non-hormonal) and the levonorgestrel IUS (hormonal, e.g. Mirena).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.front: What single factor most distinguishes the copper IUD from the IUS in the choice of method?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.back: Their effect on periods: the copper coil makes bleeding heavier/worse, whereas the hormonal IUS makes bleeding lighter and treats heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.front: What is the mechanism of action of the copper IUD?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.back: Copper ions are toxic to sperm (reduce motility and survival) and ova → prevent fertilisation; and it produces an endometrial inflammatory reaction that impairs implantation.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.front: What is the mechanism of action of the levonorgestrel IUS?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.back: Local progestogen thins/prevents proliferation of the endometrium and thickens cervical mucus. Ovulation is usually NOT suppressed (it acts locally).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.front: How effective are the copper IUD and IUS, and what two things do NOT affect their efficacy?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.back: Both are >99% effective (failure ~0.2–0.8% in year 1), not user-dependent. Efficacy is unaffected by body weight/BMI or enzyme-inducing drugs — a major advantage over pills and the implant.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.front: What is the effect of the copper IUD on periods, and its implication for menorrhagia?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.back: Periods become heavier, longer and more painful — so it is NOT recommended in heavy menstrual bleeding (worsens it). It is ideal if a woman wants a hormone-free method.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.front: What is the effect of the IUS on periods, and its role in menorrhagia?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.back: Irregular bleeding/spotting for the first ~3–6 months, then light/infrequent bleeding, often amenorrhoea, with less dysmenorrhoea. It is FIRST-LINE treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.front: How soon is the copper IUD effective after insertion?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.back: Immediately — which is why it is used as (and is the most effective) emergency contraception.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.front: How soon is the IUS effective after insertion?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.back: After 7 days (use extra cover for 7 days) — unless inserted in the first 5 days of the cycle, in which case it is immediately effective.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.front: Which intrauterine device can be used as emergency contraception, and which cannot?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.back: The copper IUD can (it is the most effective EC). The IUS cannot be used as emergency contraception.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.front: What is the licensed contraceptive duration of copper IUDs?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.back: Copper on the stem only → 5 years; copper on the stem and arms → up to 10 years.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.front: What is the updated licensed contraceptive duration of the 52 mg LNG-IUS (Mirena)?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.back: Now 8 years for contraception (updated from 5 — FSRH/licence extension, Jan 2024).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.front: For how long is the 52 mg LNG-IUS licensed as endometrial protection with oestrogen-only HRT, and were the HMB/HRT durations extended?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.back: Licensed for 4 years as the HRT progestogen (FSRH supports 5). The HMB and HRT durations were NOT extended when the contraceptive licence went to 8 years.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.front: If an IUD or IUS is inserted at what age can it be used for contraception until 55?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.back: Inserted at age ≥45 → can be used for contraception until age 55.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.front: What self-check should you teach a woman with an intrauterine device?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.back: To feel for the threads after each period, to confirm the device is still in place.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.front: What happens to fertility after removal of an IUD/IUS?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.back: There is a rapid return of fertility on removal.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.front: Over what period is the increased PID risk after IUD/IUS insertion, and what should be done beforehand?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.back: The small increase in PID risk is confined to the first ~20 days after insertion; screen for STIs beforehand. After ~20 days the risk returns to baseline.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.front: What is the approximate perforation risk with IUD/IUS insertion, and what raises it?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.back: ~1–2 per 1000. Higher with a fixed/retroverted uterus or early postpartum insertion.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.front: What is the approximate expulsion risk, and when is it highest?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.back: ~1 in 20, highest in the first few months after insertion.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.front: If pregnancy occurs with an IUD/IUS in situ, what is the key concern?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.back: A higher PROPORTION of such pregnancies are ectopic (though the absolute ectopic risk is lower than using no contraception, since overall pregnancy is rare) → always exclude an ectopic if she is pregnant.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.front: A woman with an IUD reports she can no longer feel the threads ('lost threads'). What must you consider and do?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.back: Lost threads could mean expulsion, perforation or pregnancy → exclude pregnancy first, then locate the device (ultrasound; abdominal X-ray if not seen), and advise extra contraception meanwhile.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.front: What are the general contraindications common to both the copper IUD and IUS?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.back: Current PID / current STI / puerperal or post-abortal sepsis (defer until treated); unexplained vaginal bleeding before evaluation; uterine cavity distortion (fibroids/anomalies); cervical or endometrial cancer; current gestational trophoblastic disease.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.front: Which contraindication is specific to the IUS (hormonal)?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.back: Current breast cancer.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.front: Which contraindications are specific to the copper IUD?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.back: Wilson's disease and copper allergy.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.front: Why is the IUS particularly useful in a woman who also has heavy periods or in whom you want to avoid oestrogen?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.back: It treats HMB (first-line) and, being progestogen-only and local, it avoids the oestrogen risks that matter in conditions like hypertension or VTE risk — one device solving contraception plus the coexisting problem.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.front: Does the IUS reliably suppress ovulation?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Intrauterine.back: No — the IUS acts locally (thin endometrium + thick mucus); ovulation usually continues. (Contrast with systemic combined/progestogen methods that suppress ovulation.)

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.front: What is emergency contraception (EC) used for, and what is the core principle governing oral EC?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.back: EC is used after unprotected sexual intercourse (UPSI) or contraceptive failure to prevent pregnancy. The core principle: oral EC works mainly by delaying/inhibiting ovulation — so it is ineffective once ovulation has already occurred, and useless if the woman is already pregnant.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.front: Name the three methods of emergency contraception.
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.back: Copper intrauterine device (Cu-IUD), ulipristal acetate (UPA — EllaOne), and levonorgestrel (LNG — Levonelle).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.front: Which method is the most effective emergency contraceptive, and why should it be offered to all eligible women?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.back: The copper IUD (~99% effective). It works after fertilisation (blocks implantation), so it is effective at any point in the cycle, is unaffected by weight or enzyme inducers, and can be left in for ongoing long-term contraception. It is consistently under-offered.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.front: What is the time window for copper IUD insertion as EC?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.back: Within 5 days of UPSI; OR, if later, up to 5 days after the earliest likely ovulation (≈ day 19 of a 28-day cycle).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.front: Why is the copper IUD's mechanism fundamentally different from oral EC?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.back: It is toxic to sperm/ova AND blocks implantation — a post-fertilisation effect — so unlike oral EC it works even after ovulation has occurred and at any point in the cycle.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.front: What two factors do NOT affect copper IUD efficacy, giving it an advantage over oral EC?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.back: Body weight/BMI and enzyme-inducing drugs — neither reduces its efficacy.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.front: What is ulipristal acetate (UPA / EllaOne) and its mechanism?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.back: A selective progesterone receptor modulator (SPRM) that delays ovulation — effective even close to ovulation, when LNG is already failing.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.front: What is the dose and time window for ulipristal (UPA)?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.back: A single 30 mg oral dose, as soon as possible, no later than 120 hours (5 days) after UPSI.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.front: How does BMI affect ulipristal efficacy?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.back: Reduced efficacy if BMI >30 — less weight-sensitive than LNG, but not immune. The copper IUD is preferred at high BMI.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.front: What are the key interaction rules between ulipristal (UPA) and progestogens?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.back: They interfere with each other: (1) progestogen in the 7 days before UPA can reduce its efficacy; (2) wait 5 days after UPA before starting/restarting hormonal contraception (use barriers meanwhile); (3) do not use UPA + levonorgestrel together in the same episode.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.front: In which condition should ulipristal be used with caution/avoided, and why?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.back: Severe asthma controlled by oral steroids — because of UPA's anti-progesterone effect.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.front: What is the current (FSRH 2025) advice on breastfeeding after ulipristal?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.back: No interruption of breastfeeding is needed after a single UPA dose — the old 'express and discard for 1 week' advice has been withdrawn.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.front: What is levonorgestrel (LNG / Levonelle) and its mechanism?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.back: A progestogen that inhibits/delays ovulation. The established mechanism is ovulation delay; a post-implantation effect is NOT established, and it does not disrupt an existing pregnancy.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.front: What is the dose and time window for levonorgestrel (LNG)?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.back: A single 1.5 mg oral dose as soon as possible, within 72 hours (3 days) of UPSI. Efficacy falls with time.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.front: When and how should the levonorgestrel dose be doubled?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.back: Double to 3 mg if BMI >26 or weight >70 kg (higher body weight lowers serum levels), OR if the woman is on enzyme-inducing drugs (or within the last 4 weeks) — though a copper IUD is preferred in the latter case.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.front: What should you do if a woman vomits within 3 hours of taking levonorgestrel?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.back: Repeat the dose.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.front: How does quick-starting regular hormonal contraception differ after LNG versus after UPA?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.back: After LNG: start regular hormonal contraception immediately (plus barrier cover as needed for that method). After UPA: WAIT 5 days before starting/restarting hormonal contraception (use barrier methods meanwhile), because progestogen would reduce UPA's efficacy.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.front: Can oral EC methods be used more than once in a cycle?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.back: Yes — both LNG and UPA can be used more than once in a cycle. But do not use UPA and LNG together in the same episode.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.front: When should a pregnancy test be done after taking EC?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.back: If the next period is more than 5–7 days late, or is lighter than usual.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.front: What should always accompany EC provision besides the method itself?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.back: STI risk assessment, and safeguarding — for under-16s apply Fraser guidelines.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.front: Why is the copper IUD the fallback when ovulation may already have occurred?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.back: Because oral EC only works by delaying ovulation and is ineffective once ovulation has happened; the copper IUD also blocks implantation (post-fertilisation), so it still works.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.front: What is the ranking of the three EC methods by effectiveness?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.back: Copper IUD (most effective, ~99%) > ulipristal (works closer to ovulation than LNG) > levonorgestrel (least effective; efficacy falls with time).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.front: Is there any breastfeeding restriction with levonorgestrel EC?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.back: No — LNG has no breastfeeding restriction.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.front: A woman on regular progestogen contraception took a missed-pill risk and needs EC — which oral EC is affected and how?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.back: UPA: recent progestogen (in the 7 days before) can reduce UPA's efficacy, and hormonal contraception must be delayed 5 days after UPA. LNG is not reduced by this interaction and allows immediate quick-starting — so LNG or a copper IUD may be more practical when she wants to continue/start hormonal contraception straight away.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.front: What is the brand name for ulipristal acetate and for levonorgestrel EC?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.back: Ulipristal acetate = EllaOne. Levonorgestrel = Levonelle.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.front: If a woman has a copper IUD inserted as EC but wants it removed, when should it be removed?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Emergency Con.back: Keep it in until her next period (to ensure the current cycle is covered), then remove it — or, ideally, leave it in for ongoing long-term contraception.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What type of contraceptive is the combined patch, and what is the only licensed UK product?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: It is a combined hormonal contraceptive (oestrogen + progestogen) delivered transdermally. The only UK-licensed combined patch is Evra, releasing ethinylestradiol + norelgestromin.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What is the advantage of transdermal hormone delivery in the patch?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: It bypasses first-pass hepatic metabolism, giving steady hormone levels, and (unlike the COCP) absorption is unaffected by vomiting/diarrhoea.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What is the primary mechanism of action of the contraceptive patch?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: It inhibits ovulation (oestrogen + progestogen suppress FSH/LH). Secondary effects: thickens cervical mucus and thins the endometrium.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: How effective is the patch?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Over 99% with perfect use (~91% with typical use) — the same as the COCP.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: Describe the standard patch regimen.
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Weeks 1–3: a new patch every week (same 'change day'). Week 4: a patch-free week, producing a withdrawal bleed, then start the next cycle. It can also be used in tailored/extended regimens (no patch-free week, or tricycling).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What are the starting rules for the patch and the extra-cover requirement?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Started on days 1–5 of the cycle → immediately effective. Started at any other time → 7 days of extra (barrier) cover.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What is the underlying danger that all the 'delayed patch change' rules protect against?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Extending the hormone-free interval — which allows ovulation. This mirrors the COCP's 48-hour missed-pill logic.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: A patch change at the end of Week 1 or 2 is delayed by LESS than 48 hours — what do you do?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Apply a new patch immediately; no extra precautions needed and the change day stays the same.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: A patch change at the end of Week 1 or 2 is delayed by MORE than 48 hours — what do you do?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Apply a new patch and start a NEW 4-week cycle (this becomes the new day 1/change day), plus barrier cover for 7 days. Consider emergency contraception if there was unprotected sex in the preceding 5 days or during an extended patch-free interval.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: The patch is left on too long at the end of Week 3 (over-run into the patch-free week) — what do you do?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Remove the patch as soon as possible and apply the next patch on the usual cycle start day (even if a withdrawal bleed is occurring). No additional contraception is needed.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: The first patch of a new cycle is applied late (after the patch-free week) — what is the consequence and action?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Any delay starting a new cycle extends the hormone-free interval → use additional contraception for 7 days. Consider EC if there was unprotected sex during the extended patch-free interval.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What is the unifying rule for patch problems?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: A >48-hour lapse (or a delayed start to a new cycle) means the patch may not be working → 7 days extra cover ± EC. A short (<48 h) mid-cycle lapse is covered with no extra precautions.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: A patch detaches. How does the management depend on how long it has been off?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: <48 h off: reapply (or apply a new patch) immediately, no extra cover, keep the same change day. ≥48 h off (or duration unknown): start a new cycle + 7 days extra cover ± EC. If a patch won't re-stick, apply a new one — do NOT use tape.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: Above what body weight is the patch's efficacy reduced?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: ≥90 kg — consider an alternative method.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What are the key advantages of the patch over the COCP?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Weekly rather than daily (better adherence for some), the same non-contraceptive benefits (lighter, regular, controlled cycles), and absorption is unaffected by vomiting/diarrhoea.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What oestrogen-related risks and UKMEC 4 contraindications does the patch share with the COCP?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Same oestrogen risks (VTE, arterial disease) and same UKMEC contraindications — migraine with aura, personal history of VTE, and age >35 with smoking are all UKMEC 4.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What are the disadvantages/drawbacks of the patch?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Visible; can cause skin irritation at the application site; reduced efficacy if ≥90 kg; no STI protection; and it carries the same oestrogen contraindications as the COCP.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: Does the patch protect against sexually transmitted infections?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: No — condoms are still needed for STI protection.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: Which two hormones does the Evra patch contain?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Ethinylestradiol (oestrogen) and norelgestromin (progestogen).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: If a woman using the patch vomits repeatedly, does she need extra contraceptive cover?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: No — because the hormones are absorbed transdermally, patch efficacy is unaffected by vomiting or diarrhoea (a distinct advantage over the COCP).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: Why do over-40s, postpartum women and trans/gender-diverse people need a modified contraceptive approach?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: Their physiology, risk profile or goals differ from the standard UKMEC case: over-40s have declining (but non-zero) fertility with rising VTE/cardiovascular/cancer risk; postpartum is a prothrombotic state with rapid return of fertility and breastfeeding considerations; and in trans/gender-diverse people gender-affirming hormones are NOT contraception. The same methods apply — the risk–benefit balance shifts.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: Over 40, what is the UKMEC category for combined hormonal contraception (CHC) on the basis of age alone, and up to what age can it be used?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: Age ≥40 alone is UKMEC 2 for CHC. It can be continued up to age 50 in low-risk women (non-smoking, no cardiovascular/VTE risk factors), then stopped and switched to a safer method.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: What CHC preparation is preferred in women over 40?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: A lower-dose pill: ≤30 µg ethinylestradiol combined with a levonorgestrel- or norethisterone-containing progestogen (lower VTE/cardiovascular/stroke risk than higher-dose or other progestogens).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: What non-contraceptive benefits make CHC useful in the perimenopause?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: It maintains bone mineral density, reduces vasomotor (menopausal) symptoms and controls perimenopausal menorrhagia/bleeding.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: Why is the LNG-IUS (e.g. Mirena) an excellent choice over 40?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: It provides contraception, treats coexisting heavy menstrual bleeding, and can serve as the progestogen arm of HRT — three roles in one device.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: A 52 mg LNG-IUS inserted at what age can be used for contraception until 55? And the caveat if it is the HRT progestogen?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: Inserted at ≥45 → can stay for contraception until age 55. BUT if it is being used as the progestogen component of HRT it must still be changed every 5 years.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: A copper IUD inserted at what age can remain in until the menopause?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: Inserted at ≥40 → can stay until contraception is no longer needed/menopause (then removed after 1 year of amenorrhoea if ≥50, or 2 years if <50).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: What are the concerns with prolonged DMPA (Depo) use in over-40s, and what should happen at 50?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: Concerns: bone mineral density loss and cardiovascular risk. Review over-40s regularly and, at age 50, counsel on risks/benefits and switch to an alternative method.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: At what age can ALL women stop contraception regardless of bleeding, and why?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: Age 55 — spontaneous conception is exceptionally rare beyond this even with ongoing bleeding.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: When can a non-hormonal (e.g. copper IUD/barrier) method be stopped before 55?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: After 1 year of amenorrhoea if aged ≥50, or 2 years of amenorrhoea if aged <50.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: How is the FSH test used to guide stopping a progestogen-only method?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: In someone ≥50 on a progestogen-only method, a one-off FSH in the menopausal range means contraception can stop 1 year later. FSH CANNOT be interpreted on CHC (it suppresses FSH — would need to stop CHC for 6 weeks first).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: Why is 'HRT is not contraception' a classic exam trap?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: HRT does not reliably suppress ovulation, so a perimenopausal woman on HRT still needs contraception until the appropriate stopping point (up to 55). The LNG-IUS can uniquely provide both the HRT progestogen and contraception.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: From what day postpartum is contraception needed, and why not before?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: From day 21 — ovulation can return by then. Before day 21 the earliest ovulation risk is negligible so no contraception is required.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: What extra-precaution rules apply to methods started after day 21 postpartum?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: Any method other than the POP started after day 21 → 7 days of additional precautions. A POP started after day 21 → 2 days of extra precautions.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: What is the UKMEC for CHC in the first 21 days postpartum, and why?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: UKMEC 4 (do not use) — the postpartum period is a prothrombotic state and oestrogen adds unacceptable VTE risk. With additional VTE risk factors (immobility, BMI ≥30, PPH, caesarean, pre-eclampsia, smoking) it stays UKMEC 4 up to 6 weeks.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: When can CHC be started postpartum in a NON-breastfeeding woman vs a breastfeeding woman?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: Non-breastfeeding, no VTE risk factors: from day 21 (UKMEC 2). Breastfeeding: from 6 weeks (UKMEC <6 weeks is 4; 6 weeks–6 months is 2). Oestrogen may also reduce milk supply.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: What is the UKMEC for progestogen-only methods (POP, implant, DMPA) postpartum, including while breastfeeding?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: UKMEC 1 — safe from birth, including in breastfeeding; can be started immediately. Only a small amount of progestogen enters milk and it is harmless to the infant.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: What are the two permitted timing windows for IUD/IUS insertion postpartum, and what is the window between them?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: Insert within 48 hours of delivery, OR wait until ≥4 weeks. The 48 hours–4 weeks window is UKMEC 3 (avoid) because of increased expulsion and ~6-fold perforation risk.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: What three criteria must ALL be met for the lactational amenorrhoea method (LAM) to be ~98% effective?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: Fully/exclusively breastfeeding + amenorrhoeic + under 6 months postpartum. Efficacy falls once any one fails (supplementary feeds, periods return, or >6 months).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: After miscarriage, abortion or ectopic, from what day is contraception needed and when can methods start?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: Contraception is needed from day 5; methods can usually be started immediately.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: What is the single most important principle for contraception in trans/gender-diverse people?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: Gender-affirming hormone therapy is NOT contraception. Pregnancy (or causing pregnancy) remains possible, so contraceptive need is assessed by anatomy and sexual activity, not gender identity.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: Does testosterone prevent pregnancy in a trans man / person assigned female at birth, and what is the key teratogenic concern?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: No — testosterone often causes amenorrhoea but does NOT prevent pregnancy. It is teratogenic (virilises an XX fetus), so effective contraception is essential and testosterone must not be relied upon.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: Which contraceptive methods are preferred in a person on testosterone, and why?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: Progestogen-only methods (POP, implant, IUS) and the copper IUD — they contain no oestrogen, so they don't oppose masculinisation. Progestogens can also aid menstrual suppression/dysphoria. Testosterone should be continued alongside, not stopped.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: Why is CHC often avoided (though not absolutely contraindicated) in a person on testosterone?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: Testosterone itself is not an absolute contraindication, but oestrogen opposes masculinisation and carries a theoretical VTE concern — so many prefer to avoid oestrogen-containing methods.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: Does oestradiol/feminising therapy in a trans woman prevent pregnancy?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: No — oestradiol impairs spermatogenesis but does NOT reliably prevent pregnancy. If fertile sperm may persist (no vasectomy/orchidectomy) and having vaginal sex with pregnancy risk, contraception (barrier/partner method) is still needed. GnRH analogues also cannot be relied on.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: What counselling points are important for trans/gender-diverse people beyond contraception?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: Inclusive, affirming, individualised care; discuss fertility and fertility preservation; STI protection with condoms (including for anal/other sex); cervical screening if a cervix is present; and awareness that examinations/menstruation may cause dysphoria.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What is the contraceptive injection, and its three distinctive drawbacks?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: A long-acting progestogen given by injection every ~12 weeks (a LARC, oestrogen-free). Its three examinable drawbacks are: an irreversible ~3-month duration once given, delayed return of fertility (up to a year), and an effect on bone mineral density.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What is the main agent, dose, and route of the contraceptive injection?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Depo-Provera — medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) 150 mg — given by deep IM injection every 12 weeks.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What is Sayana Press, and its advantages?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: A subcutaneous DMPA (104 mg), bioequivalent and self-administered — useful in obesity or bleeding disorders/anticoagulation.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What is the '14-week window' for the injection?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: It can be given up to 14 weeks after the last dose without needing extra precautions (i.e. up to 2 weeks late is fine).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What is the primary mechanism of the contraceptive injection?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Inhibition of ovulation (suppressing the hypothalamic-pituitary axis so there is no LH surge) — and unlike the traditional POP, this ovulation inhibition is reliable.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What are the secondary mechanisms of the injection?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Thickening cervical mucus and thinning the endometrium.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: How and where is Depo-Provera administered?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: By deep IM injection every 12 weeks — gluteal (preferred, especially if obese), deltoid, or lateral thigh; Sayana Press is subcutaneous (abdomen/thigh).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: When does the injection give immediate cover vs needing extra protection?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Days 1–5 of the cycle → immediately effective; any other time → 7 days additional contraception (and exclude pregnancy).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What is the rule for a repeat injection given on time (≤14 weeks) vs overdue (>14 weeks)?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: ≤14 weeks since last dose → just give the next injection, no extra cover. >14 weeks (overdue) → exclude pregnancy and use extra cover for 7 days.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What are the advantages of the contraceptive injection?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Highly effective LARC (perfect-use failure ~0.2%), not user-dependent between injections; oestrogen-free (usable with VTE history, migraine with aura); only needed every 12 weeks; private; reduces menstrual pain; often causes amenorrhoea; may help HMB and endometriosis; and reduces PID/ovarian/endometrial cancer risk.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What are the disadvantages of the contraceptive injection?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: It cannot be reversed once given (effects last ~3 months, so side effects persist), delayed return of fertility (up to ~12 months), no STI protection, and it is unsuitable if injections cannot be attended reliably.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: How long can the return of fertility be delayed after stopping the injection?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Up to ~12 months (median time to conception ~9–10 months).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What is the classic side effect most associated with the contraceptive injection?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Weight gain (~2–3 kg over the first year) — the method most clearly associated with weight gain.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What bleeding pattern is seen with the injection?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Irregular bleeding is common early, but many women progress to amenorrhoea with continued use.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What progestogenic side effects can the injection cause?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Headache, mood changes/depression, breast tenderness, reduced libido, and acne.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What is the effect of DMPA on bone mineral density?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: It reduces bone mineral density (by lowering oestrogen), potentially increasing osteoporosis risk; loss is greatest in the first 1–2 years then plateaus, and is largely recovered after stopping.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What are the age caveats for DMPA related to its BMD effect?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: It is UKMEC 2 in adolescents (<18, used when other methods are unsuitable) and warrants a review of benefits/risks in women ≥50 (encourage an alternative) and those with osteoporosis risk factors; there is no restriction on duration for women 18–45 otherwise eligible.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What is the UKMEC 4 (do not use) condition for the contraceptive injection?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Current breast cancer.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: List UKMEC 3 conditions for the contraceptive injection.
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Past breast cancer, multiple cardiovascular risk factors, current IHD/stroke, and — distinctively for DMPA — significant risk factors for osteoporosis (given the BMD effect).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: Give the three signature drawbacks of the contraceptive injection.
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: (1) It is irreversible for ~3 months once given; (2) delayed return of fertility up to ~1 year; (3) reduced bone mineral density.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What is the contraceptive implant?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: A small progestogen-only rod inserted under the skin of the upper arm, giving 3 years of highly effective contraception. It is the single most effective contraceptive method (more effective than sterilisation), a LARC, and oestrogen-free.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What is the device, its hormone, and how long it lasts?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Nexplanon — a single rod containing 68 mg etonogestrel (a progestogen), released slowly over 3 years.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: Why is Nexplanon radiopaque, and what is the advantage over Implanon?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: It contains barium sulphate, making it visible on X-ray/imaging so it can be located if impalpable — the key advantage over the older Implanon.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What is the primary mechanism of action of the implant?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Inhibition of ovulation — etonogestrel suppresses the LH surge, reaching ovulation-inhibiting levels within ~1 day of insertion.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What are the secondary mechanisms of the implant?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Thickening cervical mucus (a barrier to sperm) and thinning the endometrium.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: Where and how is the implant inserted?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Subdermally in the proximal, non-dominant upper arm, overlying the triceps (medial aspect), by a trained professional.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: When can the implant be inserted with immediate cover vs needing extra protection?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Days 1–5 of the cycle → immediately effective, no extra cover. Any other time → 7 days additional contraception (and exclude pregnancy).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: Can the implant be inserted after abortion, miscarriage or birth?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Yes — it can be inserted immediately following an abortion or miscarriage, or postpartum.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: How quickly does fertility return after implant removal?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Rapidly — etonogestrel clears within ~a week of removal.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What are the advantages of the implant?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: The most effective method (failure <0.1 per 100 women over 3 years, not user-dependent); long-acting (3 years); oestrogen-free (usable with VTE history, migraine with aura); rapidly reversible; immediate post-abortion/miscarriage/postpartum insertion; and it may reduce dysmenorrhoea.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What are the disadvantages of the implant?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Requires a trained professional to insert/remove; no STI protection; 7 days extra cover if not inserted on days 1–5; irregular bleeding (the main drawback); and rare risks (implant migration, neurovascular injury at insertion, difficult removal if placed too deep).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What is the main adverse effect and commonest reason for discontinuing the implant?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Irregular/unpredictable bleeding — ranging from amenorrhoea (welcome) to frequent/prolonged bleeding; about half achieve amenorrhoea or an acceptable pattern, and the first 6 months don't reliably predict the later pattern.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: How is problematic bleeding on the implant managed?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: First exclude other causes (speculum exam + STI/chlamydia check, consider cervical pathology if persistent); then a trial of co-prescribed COCP (1–3 months) can settle it (or mefenamic acid/tranexamic acid/a progestogen).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What progestogenic side effects can the implant cause?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Headache, nausea, breast pain/tenderness, mood changes, and acne.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What is the implant's effect on bone mineral density, and the contrast with the injectable?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: No significant effect on bone mineral density — unlike the injectable (Depo), which reduces BMD (a useful contrast).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: Which drugs reduce the efficacy of the implant?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Enzyme-inducing drugs — rifampicin, some anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, phenytoin), and St John's Wort — so an additional/alternative method (often a copper IUD) is used.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: What is the UKMEC 4 (do not use) condition for the implant?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Current breast cancer.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: List UKMEC 3 conditions for the implant.
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Ischaemic heart disease/stroke developing on the method, unexplained/suspicious vaginal bleeding (before evaluation), past breast cancer, and severe (decompensated) liver cirrhosis or liver cancer.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: Why is the implant broadly usable across most medical conditions?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: Because it is oestrogen-free, so it avoids the oestrogen-related risks that limit combined methods — most conditions are UKMEC 1–2.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.front: Give the reflex for a woman with a VTE history or migraine with aura who wants highly effective contraception.
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraceptive.back: The implant is ideal — it is oestrogen-free (so usable despite these oestrogen contraindications) and is the single most effective method.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: What is the examinable skill in the contraception overview?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: Knowing the categories of method, how effectiveness is measured, the cross-cutting rules, and how to structure a counselling conversation to match a method to the individual (preferences, UKMEC eligibility, circumstances).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: What is the Pearl Index?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: Pregnancies per 100 woman-years of use — a lower value means more effective (e.g. a Pearl Index of 0.2 = 2 pregnancies per 1000 women per year).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: What is the difference between perfect use and typical use?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: Perfect use is correct and consistent use; typical use is real-world use including errors. The gap is large for user-dependent methods (pills) and negligible for LARC.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: What is the most useful way to categorise contraceptive methods, and why?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: By whether they depend on the user remembering something — LARC vs user-dependent — because this drives real-world effectiveness and the 'LARC-first' counselling emphasis.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: What are the LARC ('fit and forget') methods?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: The progestogen implant (Nexplanon), the levonorgestrel IUS, the copper IUD, and the injectable (Depo-Provera/DMPA).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: Which is the single most effective contraceptive method?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: The progestogen implant (Nexplanon).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: What are the short-acting hormonal (user-dependent) methods?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: Combined methods (COCP, combined patch/Evra, vaginal ring) and progestogen-only (POP).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: Which contraceptive methods protect against STIs?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: Only barrier methods (male/female condoms) — no other method protects against STIs.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: What are the emergency contraception options, and which is most effective?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: Levonorgestrel, ulipristal acetate, and the copper IUD — the copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraception.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: What are the permanent contraceptive methods?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: Female sterilisation (tubal occlusion) and vasectomy.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: What is the mechanism of combined hormonal contraception?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: Primarily inhibits ovulation (suppressing FSH/LH), plus thickening cervical mucus and thinning the endometrium.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: What is the mechanism of progestogen-only methods?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: Mainly thickening cervical mucus and thinning the endometrium; ovulation inhibition varies — reliable with the desogestrel POP, implant and injectable, but NOT the traditional POP.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: What is the mechanism of the copper IUD?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: Copper is toxic to sperm and ova (and impairs implantation) — it is non-hormonal.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: What is the mechanism of the LNG-IUS?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: Local progestogen thins the endometrium and thickens cervical mucus.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: What is the cross-cutting rule for contraception in active breast cancer?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: All hormonal contraception is contraindicated — only barrier methods or the copper IUD may be used.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: How is the combined patch (Evra) used?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: Worn and changed weekly for 3 weeks, then a patch-free week (withdrawal bleed) — the only combined patch licensed in the UK.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: What is the rule for a delayed patch change of ≤48h (weeks 1–2) vs >48h?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: ≤48h: change immediately, no extra cover. >48h: change + 7 days of barrier cover + consider EC if there was unprotected sex in the last 5 days or during an extended patch-free interval.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: How do the Evra patch rules relate to the COCP?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: They mirror the COCP 48-hour logic — the danger is again lengthening the hormone-free interval.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: Outline the structure of a contraception counselling conversation.
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: 1) Explore needs/preferences (reversibility, future fertility, non-daily/LARC, STI protection, non-contraceptive benefits); 2) assess UKMEC eligibility (focused history); 3) explain options (effectiveness, use, side effects, STI protection); 4) support informed choice (LARC most effective, decision aids); 5) safety-net (missed-method rules, EC, follow-up); 6) confidentiality/young people (Fraser guidelines for under-16s).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: What focused history assesses UKMEC eligibility?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: VTE/thrombophilia, migraine with aura, smoking with age >35, breast cancer, BP/BMI, breastfeeding, liver disease, and enzyme-inducing drugs.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: What guidelines apply to contraceptive advice for under-16s?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: Fraser guidelines — assessing the young person's competence to consent to contraceptive advice/treatment.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.front: Which groups modify the standard contraceptive counselling approach?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Contraception.back: Women over 40, the postpartum period, and trans/non-binary people (covered in the dedicated special-groups note).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.front: What is the COCP, and what does the topic hinge on?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.back: A combined hormonal contraceptive containing both oestrogen (ethinylestradiol) and a progestogen. The topic hinges on three things: how it works, who can't have it (UKMEC 3/4), and what to do when pills are missed.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.front: What is the primary mechanism of the COCP?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.back: It inhibits ovulation — oestrogen + progestogen suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary axis (↓FSH/LH), preventing the LH surge and ovulation.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.front: What are the secondary mechanisms of the COCP?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.back: Thickening cervical mucus (progestogen) and thinning the endometrium.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.front: How effective is the COCP, and how is efficacy measured?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.back: Over 99% effective with perfect use (~91% with typical use); efficacy is measured by the Pearl Index (pregnancies per 100 woman-years).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.front: When can the COCP be started with immediate cover vs needing extra protection?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.back: Started within the first 5 days of the cycle → immediately effective, no extra cover. Started any other time → 7 days of additional (barrier) contraception (exclude pregnancy first).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.front: What COCP regimens are available?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.back: Traditional 21/7 (one pill daily for 21 days then a 7-day pill-free interval with a withdrawal bleed) and tailored/extended regimens (equally safe) — tricycling (3 packs then a break) or continuous (no pill-free interval).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.front: What situations reduce COCP efficacy?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.back: Vomiting within 2 hours of a pill (treat as missed); drugs causing vomiting/diarrhoea (orlistat); and liver enzyme-inducing drugs (rifampicin, some anticonvulsants, St John's Wort) — use an additional/alternative method.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.front: What counts as a 'missed' COCP pill?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.back: A pill taken more than 24 hours late (i.e. >48 hours since the last one).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.front: What is the action if ONE COCP pill is missed?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.back: Take the missed pill as soon as possible (even if that means two in one day), continue as normal, and no extra contraception is needed.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.front: What is the action if TWO or more COCP pills are missed?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.back: Take the most recent missed pill ASAP (discard earlier missed ones), continue the pack, use condoms/abstain until 7 consecutive pills have been taken, then apply the 'week rule'.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.front: What is the 'week rule' for 2+ missed COCP pills in week 1 (days 1–7)?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.back: Consider emergency contraception if unprotected sex occurred in the pill-free interval or during week 1.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.front: What is the 'week rule' for 2+ missed COCP pills in week 2 (days 8–14)?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.back: No emergency contraception is needed (provided the preceding 7 days were taken correctly).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.front: What is the 'week rule' for 2+ missed COCP pills in week 3 (days 15–21)?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.back: Finish the current pack and start the next pack immediately — OMIT the pill-free interval.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.front: What is the underlying logic of the missed-pill rules?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.back: The danger is extending the hormone-free interval (which allows ovulation to escape); this is why week 1 (adjacent to the break) is riskiest and why in week 3 you skip the break to avoid a long gap.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.front: What do the UKMEC categories 1–4 mean?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.back: 1 = no restriction; 2 = benefits outweigh risks; 3 = risks generally outweigh benefits (avoid unless no alternative); 4 = unacceptable risk (do NOT use).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.front: List examples of UKMEC 3 conditions for the COCP.
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.back: Age >35 and smoking <15/day, BMI >35, a first-degree relative with VTE <45, controlled hypertension, immobility, BRCA1/2 carrier, and current gallbladder disease.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.front: List the UKMEC 4 (absolute) contraindications to the COCP.
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.back: Migraine WITH aura (any age), age >35 and smoking ≥15/day, history of VTE or a thrombogenic mutation (Factor V Leiden), history of stroke or ischaemic heart disease, breastfeeding <6 weeks postpartum, uncontrolled hypertension, current breast cancer, major surgery with prolonged immobilisation, and positive antiphospholipid antibodies.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.front: Why is migraine with aura a UKMEC 4 contraindication to the COCP?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.back: Because of the increased stroke risk — it is the classic UKMEC 4 answer (any age).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.front: What is the surgery rule for the COCP?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.back: Stop oestrogen-containing contraception 4 weeks before major/immobilising surgery, because of the VTE risk.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.front: What contraception can be used in active breast cancer?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.back: Only barrier methods or the copper IUD — all hormonal contraception is contraindicated.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.front: What are the advantages of the COCP?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.back: Highly effective, reversible, doesn't interfere with sex; lighter, more regular, less painful periods (good for HMB, dysmenorrhoea, PMS); reduces ovarian, endometrial and colorectal cancer; protects against PID; and may reduce ovarian cysts, benign breast disease and acne.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.front: What are the disadvantages/risks of the COCP?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.back: No STI protection; user-dependent; increased risk of VTE, breast cancer, cervical cancer, ischaemic heart disease and stroke; and temporary side effects (headache, nausea, breast tenderness, mood changes, spotting).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.front: What is the elegant mnemonic for COCP and cancer risk?
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Combined Oral.back: The COCP raises the risk of the cancers we screen for (breast, cervical) and protects against the ones we don't (ovarian, endometrial).

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.question: A 38-year-old woman who smokes and has a history of DVT wants an oral contraceptive. The combined pill is unsuitable. What is the most appropriate oral option and why?
options: Combined oral contraceptive pill at a lower dose
Progestogen-only pill — it contains no oestrogen so avoids the VTE and smoking-related risks
No oral contraceptive can be used
Combined patch, as transdermal oestrogen is safe
Ulipristal acetate taken regularly
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.answer: Progestogen-only pill — it contains no oestrogen so avoids the VTE and smoking-related risks
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.explanation: The POP contains no oestrogen, so it avoids the oestrogen-related VTE and arterial risks that make the COCP UKMEC 4 in a >35 smoker with a VTE history. It is usable in almost everyone and is the appropriate oral choice here. The patch and COCP both contain oestrogen and share the same contraindications.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.question: A woman taking the traditional (levonorgestrel) progestogen-only pill realises she took today's pill 5 hours late. What is the correct advice?
options: No action needed — she is still protected
Take it now and use condoms until she has taken pills correctly for 48 hours; consider EC if she had UPSI
Take two pills now and skip tomorrow's
Stop the pill and wait for her period
Use condoms for 7 days
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.answer: Take it now and use condoms until she has taken pills correctly for 48 hours; consider EC if she had UPSI
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.explanation: The traditional POP window is 3 hours; at 5 hours late it is a missed pill. She should take it as soon as possible, continue the pack, use condoms until 48 hours of correct pill-taking (time for cervical mucus to re-thicken), and consider emergency contraception if she had unprotected sex during the unprotected window.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.question: A woman on the desogestrel POP (Cerazette) took her pill 10 hours late. What is the correct advice?
options: It is a missed pill — use condoms for 48 hours
No extra precautions are needed — desogestrel allows up to a 12-hour window
She needs emergency contraception immediately
She must restart a new pack
Use condoms for 7 days
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.answer: No extra precautions are needed — desogestrel allows up to a 12-hour window
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.explanation: The desogestrel POP has a 12-hour window (its anovulatory action gives a wider margin). At 10 hours late she is still within the window, so she simply takes the pill and needs no additional precautions. It would only be a missed pill if taken >12 hours late.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.question: A woman starts the progestogen-only pill on day 8 of her cycle. What advice about additional contraception should she receive?
options: Immediate protection — no extra cover needed
Use additional contraception for 48 hours
Use additional contraception for 7 days
Wait until her next period before relying on it
Use additional contraception for 24 hours
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.explanation: Started up to and including day 5, the POP gives immediate protection. Started at any other time (here day 8), 48 hours of additional contraception are needed for the cervical mucus to thicken sufficiently.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.question: A woman on the progestogen-only pill is prescribed a 5-day course of amoxicillin for a chest infection. What is the correct advice about her contraception?
options: Use condoms during and for 7 days after the antibiotics
No additional precautions are needed — ordinary antibiotics do not reduce POP efficacy
Stop the POP until the antibiotics finish
Take a double dose of the POP while on antibiotics
Switch to the copper IUD for the duration
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.answer: No additional precautions are needed — ordinary antibiotics do not reduce POP efficacy
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.explanation: Non-enzyme-inducing (ordinary) antibiotics such as amoxicillin do NOT reduce the efficacy of the POP — a common misconception. No extra precautions are needed. Only enzyme-inducing drugs (e.g. rifampicin) reduce efficacy.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.question: A woman with epilepsy taking carbamazepine wants the progestogen-only pill. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: The POP is fully effective with carbamazepine
Carbamazepine is an enzyme inducer that reduces POP efficacy; a non-hormonal method (e.g. copper IUD) is preferred
Double the POP dose to compensate
Ordinary antibiotics are the only interaction to worry about
Switch her to the combined pill instead
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.answer: Carbamazepine is an enzyme inducer that reduces POP efficacy; a non-hormonal method (e.g. copper IUD) is preferred
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.explanation: Carbamazepine is an enzyme-inducing anticonvulsant that reduces the efficacy of the POP (and other hormonal pills/implant). A method unaffected by enzyme inducers — ideally a non-hormonal option such as the copper IUD, or the IUS — is preferred.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.question: A 29-year-old woman started on the traditional POP 4 months ago reports ongoing unpredictable spotting. She is otherwise well. What is the most appropriate initial approach?
options: Immediately stop the POP as it has failed
Reassure that irregular bleeding is the commonest side effect, but as it persists >3 months, exclude other causes (pregnancy, STI, cervical pathology)
Add oestrogen tablets to control the bleeding
Switch straight to the copper IUD
Prescribe long-term tranexamic acid
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.answer: Reassure that irregular bleeding is the commonest side effect, but as it persists >3 months, exclude other causes (pregnancy, STI, cervical pathology)
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.explanation: Irregular vaginal bleeding is the most common POP side effect and the leading reason for discontinuation. It often settles, but because it has persisted beyond 3 months, other causes (pregnancy, STI, cervical/endometrial pathology) should be excluded before attributing it to the pill and considering a switch.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.question: Which statement about the mechanism of the traditional progestogen-only pill is correct?
options: It reliably inhibits ovulation in every cycle
It works mainly by thickening cervical mucus; ovulation is inhibited in only about 50–60% of cycles
It works by delivering oestrogen locally
Its main action is preventing implantation
It suppresses FSH and LH as effectively as the COCP
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.answer: It works mainly by thickening cervical mucus; ovulation is inhibited in only about 50–60% of cycles
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.explanation: The traditional POP works mainly by thickening cervical mucus (with endometrial thinning and reduced tubal motility); it inhibits ovulation in only ~50–60% of cycles. This short-lived mucus effect is why timing is strict (3-hour window). Desogestrel/drospirenone POPs additionally inhibit ovulation reliably.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.question: A woman with current breast cancer requests the progestogen-only pill. What is the correct advice?
options: The POP is safe as it contains no oestrogen
Current breast cancer is UKMEC 4 for the POP — it should not be used; offer a non-hormonal method
She can use it if the cancer is hormone-receptor negative
Only the combined pill is contraindicated, not the POP
She can use the POP at half dose
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.answer: Current breast cancer is UKMEC 4 for the POP — it should not be used; offer a non-hormonal method
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.explanation: Current breast cancer is the main UKMEC 4 (absolute) contraindication to the POP, because it is hormone-sensitive. A non-hormonal method (e.g. copper IUD) should be offered. Past breast cancer is UKMEC 3.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.question: A woman on the traditional POP becomes pregnant and presents with lower abdominal pain. What is the key clinical concern?
options: The pregnancy is certainly intrauterine
A slightly higher proportion of pregnancies on the traditional POP are ectopic, so an ectopic must be excluded
The POP causes miscarriage so no action is needed
She should simply stop the POP and be reviewed in a month
Pain always means normal implantation
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.answer: A slightly higher proportion of pregnancies on the traditional POP are ectopic, so an ectopic must be excluded
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.explanation: Because the traditional POP does not always suppress ovulation, a slightly higher proportion of pregnancies that occur are ectopic. A POP user who becomes pregnant with abdominal pain must have an ectopic excluded, even though any contraception lowers the absolute ectopic risk compared with using none.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.question: A woman wishes to switch from the COCP to the POP without a gap in protection. What is the correct advice?
options: Take a 7-day break, then start the POP
Start the POP immediately after the last active COCP pill (straight after day 21, no gap) for immediate protection
Start the POP during the pill-free week for immediate cover
She always needs 7 days of extra cover when switching
She cannot switch directly and must use condoms for a month
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.answer: Start the POP immediately after the last active COCP pill (straight after day 21, no gap) for immediate protection
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.explanation: Continuing directly from the end of an active COCP packet (immediately after day 21, with no pill-free gap) gives immediate protection when switching to the POP. Starting during or after a pill-free interval would require additional cover.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.question: A breastfeeding woman 3 weeks postpartum wants a reliable oral contraceptive. What is the most appropriate advice about the POP?
options: The POP is contraindicated in breastfeeding
The POP is safe in breastfeeding (UKMEC 1) and can be started now; only a small, harmless amount enters milk
She must wait until 6 weeks as with the combined pill
The POP reduces milk supply significantly
She should use the combined pill instead while breastfeeding
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.answer: The POP is safe in breastfeeding (UKMEC 1) and can be started now; only a small, harmless amount enters milk
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.explanation: The POP is UKMEC 1 in breastfeeding and can be started immediately postpartum; only a small amount of progestogen enters breast milk and it is harmless to the infant. (Combined methods, by contrast, are avoided early postpartum and while breastfeeding under 6 weeks.)

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.question: A woman on the traditional POP vomits 90 minutes after taking her pill. What is the correct advice?
options: Nothing further is needed as it was likely absorbed
Treat it as a missed pill — take another pill as soon as she can and use condoms until 48 hours of correct pill-taking
Take two extra pills to be safe
Stop the POP for the rest of the pack
Switch to the combined pill
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.answer: Treat it as a missed pill — take another pill as soon as she can and use condoms until 48 hours of correct pill-taking
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.explanation: Vomiting within 2 hours of taking the POP (or severe diarrhoea) is treated as a missed pill because absorption may be incomplete. She should take another pill as soon as possible, continue the pack, and use condoms until pills have been taken correctly for 48 hours.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.question: Which progestogen-only pill has the longest missed-pill window and what is that window?
options: Levonorgestrel POP — 3 hours
Desogestrel POP (Cerazette) — 12 hours
Drospirenone POP (Slynd) — 24 hours
Norethisterone POP — 6 hours
All POPs share a 3-hour window
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.explanation: The drospirenone POP (Slynd) has the longest window at 24 hours (and a 4-day hormone-free interval with its own rules). Desogestrel is 12 hours and traditional POPs (levonorgestrel, norethisterone) are 3 hours.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.question: A 32-year-old woman with migraine with aura wants oral contraception. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: The COCP is fine at a low dose
The combined pill is UKMEC 4 (stroke risk); the POP contains no oestrogen and is a suitable oral option
No oral contraception is safe with migraine with aura
She should use the combined patch instead
Migraine with aura contraindicates the POP as well
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.answer: The combined pill is UKMEC 4 (stroke risk); the POP contains no oestrogen and is a suitable oral option
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.explanation: Migraine with aura is UKMEC 4 for combined (oestrogen-containing) methods because of ischaemic stroke risk. The POP contains no oestrogen and is a suitable oral alternative, being usable in almost everyone including this group.

conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.question: A woman on the POP misses two consecutive pills. What is the correct action regarding the missed pills?
options: Take both missed pills together, then continue
Take just one pill (the most recent) as soon as possible, continue the pack at the usual time, and use condoms until 48 hours of correct pills
Discard the pack and start a new one
Take three pills to catch up
Stop and wait for her period before restarting
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.answer: Take just one pill (the most recent) as soon as possible, continue the pack at the usual time, and use condoms until 48 hours of correct pills
conditions__CONTRACEPTION__Progestogen-O.explanation: If more than one POP is missed, she takes only one pill (the most recent) as soon as she remembers, continues the pack at the usual time, uses condoms until pills have been taken correctly for 48 hours, and considers emergency contraception if she had unprotected sex during the unprotected window.
